name: Xoxocotlán International Airport
before:
Oaxaca's airport, in the southern suburb of Santa Cruz Xoxocotlán, and one of the faster growing in Mexico as the city's popularity has risen. It carried 1,864,967 passengers in 2025, up on 1,787,428 the year before.

It is a single storey terminal of 7,548 square metres handling both domestic and international flights, with eight gates that open straight onto the apron. There are no air bridges here, so passengers walk out to the aircraft along open air walkways, which is worth knowing when a client is travelling with young children or in the rain.

The runway is 2,450 metres at an elevation of 1,521 metres, with nine stands for narrow bodied aircraft and room for up to 22 movements an hour.

The airport is run by ASUR and is the hub for the regional airline Aerotucán. It also hosts Mexican Army facilities, courier operations and flight training.

The name comes from the Nahuatl word xocotl, meaning a sour or sweet and sour fruit.
after:
Oaxaca's airport, officially Xoxocotlán International Airport, stands in a southern suburb of the city. It carried 1,864,967 passengers in 2025, up on 1,787,428 the year before.

Its terminal, of 7,548 square metres, handles both domestic and international flights. Aeroméxico, Viva Aerobus, Volaris and United fly here.

The runway is 2,450 metres at an elevation of 1,521 metres, with room for up to 22 movements an hour.

ASUR runs the airport, which also has a general aviation building for small private aircraft.

claims.claim: one of the faster growing in Mexico
claims.wasBefore: and one of the faster growing in Mexico as the city's popularity has risen
claims.why: Wikipedia alone, and not borne out by 2025: Oaxaca grew 4.3 per cent, less than Mérida (6.5) and Veracruz (9.3) among ASUR's own airports (ASUR, January 2026). The passenger totals are kept.

claims.wasBefore: in the southern suburb of Santa Cruz Xoxocotlán
claims.why: The municipality rests on Wikipedia alone; ASUR gives only the road address. Softened to 'a southern suburb', which the coordinates confirm, and the official name Xoxocotlán is kept.

claims.wasBefore: It is a single storey terminal
claims.why: Sources disagree: Wikipedia says single-storey, while ASUR's airport map shows Terminal 1 with a first and a second floor. The area is kept.

claims.claim: eight gates straight onto the apron
claims.wasBefore: with eight gates that open straight onto the apron
claims.why: Wikipedia alone for the gate count. ASUR's annual report gives the terminal nine contact positions and its technical page six Code C stands, all at the terminal and none remote.

claims.claim: no air bridges; walk to the aircraft
claims.wasBefore: There are no air bridges here, so passengers walk out to the aircraft along open air walkways, which is worth knowing when a client is travelling with young children or in the rain.
claims.why: Wikipedia alone. ASUR's annual report names boarding bridges or telescopic corridors at its other airports and none at Oaxaca (nine contact positions), which suggests there are none but does not say so. A practical point worth restoring if ASUR or a second source states it.

claims.wasBefore: with nine stands for narrow bodied aircraft
claims.why: Sources disagree: Wikipedia has nine stands mainly for narrow-bodies and ASUR's annual report nine contact positions, but ASUR's technical page gives six Code C stands (or four C and one D).

claims.wasBefore: and is the hub for the regional airline Aerotucán
claims.why: No current source: Aerotucán's .com.mx site shows a WordPress critical error, the aerotucan.com route page Wikipedia cites is a 404, and neither ASUR's airline list nor El Universal's October 2025 list of direct routes mentions it. Replaced by the airlines both sources name.

claims.claim: Army facilities, courier operations and flight training
claims.wasBefore: It also hosts Mexican Army facilities, courier operations and flight training.
claims.why: Wikipedia alone (its own body text describes Air Force Base No. 15, not the Army). SEDENA's page on gob.mx answers with an Akamai challenge page. The general aviation building is kept (ASUR).

claims.wasBefore: The name comes from the Nahuatl word xocotl, meaning a sour or sweet and sour fruit.
claims.why: Only Wikipedia ties the name to xocotl. The Online Nahuatl Dictionary (University of Oregon) confirms xocotl means 'a sour fruit; or, fruit in general' but not 'sweet and sour', and has no entry for Xoxocotlán; INAFED's municipal encyclopedia did not answer.
Held back: ASUR's technical page gives Oaxaca's operating hours as 0600-2000. One source, and a fact the old text has nothing to replace; useful for late arrivals if Andy wants it.

sources.quote: 1,521 m (4,990 ft) Largest aircraft: MD11 Runway capacity – operations per hour: 22 Operating hours: 0600-2000

claims.claim: Hurricane Polo warning, week of 21 September 2026
claims.why: Held back: the FCDO (updated 22 September 2026) reports Hurricane Polo bringing heavy rain to parts of Guerrero, Michoacán and Oaxaca states in the week of 21 September, with a hurricane warning in place. Transient, and nothing in the old text to replace; flagged in case clients are travelling now.

quote: Hurricane Polo is bringing heavy rainfall across Mexico’s southwestern coast, including parts of Guerrero, Michoacan and Oaxaca states.
